reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: A claw toe shows hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal joint combined with flexion at both the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints
This combined pattern distinguishes it from hammer toe (mainly proximal interphalangeal flexion) and mallet toe (isolated distal interphalangeal flexion)
Clawing usually affects several toes simultaneously and is frequently bilateral, which should raise suspicion of a neuromuscular cause
Underlying associations include Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other peripheral neuropathies, cavus foot, diabetic neuropathy, and inflammatory arthritis
Metatarsophalangeal hyperextension drives the metatarsal head plantarward, producing painful plantar callosities and metatarsalgia, while dorsal corns form over the flexed toes
Flexibility should be assessed, as passively correctable clawing can be treated with tendon balancing whereas fixed deformity needs bony correction
Conservative care includes accommodative deep-toe-box footwear, metatarsal offloading orthoses, toe splints, and callus care
Because clawing is often part of a wider foot deformity, examine for cavus and neurological signs and treat the whole foot rather than the toe alone
reference.pathophysiology: Claw toe results from a muscle imbalance in which the intrinsic muscles of the foot are weak or fail to counterbalance the long extrinsic tendons. The long extensor hyperextends the metatarsophalangeal joint while the long flexor flexes both interphalangeal joints, producing the characteristic clawed posture across several toes. Because the deforming mechanism frequently reflects generalised intrinsic weakness, clawing is strongly linked to neuromuscular disorders such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other peripheral neuropathies, and to cavus foot deformity, diabetes, and inflammatory arthritis. The hyperextended metatarsophalangeal joint drives the metatarsal head into a plantarflexed and prominent position, increasing plantar pressure and causing metatarsalgia and callosities, while the dorsally elevated interphalangeal joints rub against footwear. Initially flexible, the deformity becomes fixed as capsular and tendon contractures develop.
additionalDifferentials: Hammer toe with predominant proximal interphalangeal flexion
Mallet toe with isolated distal interphalangeal flexion
Cavus foot deformity with associated toe clawing
Rheumatoid or other inflammatory forefoot deformity
Diabetic or other peripheral neuropathy with intrinsic wasting
Compartment syndrome sequelae producing intrinsic contracture
Freiberg's infraction contributing to lesser-toe symptoms
additionalInvestigations: Standing clinical examination defining metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal posture and flexibility
Weight-bearing foot radiographs to assess metatarsophalangeal subluxation and cavus alignment
Detailed neurological examination for peripheral neuropathy and intrinsic muscle wasting
Nerve conduction studies or referral for neurological assessment where a neuromuscular cause is suspected
Screening for diabetes and assessment of protective sensation
Pedobarography to quantify forefoot overload and callosity distribution
Inflammatory markers and serology if inflammatory arthritis is considered
redFlags: Bilateral or progressive clawing with a cavus foot suggesting Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or another hereditary neuropathy
Sensory loss with plantar ulceration in a neuropathic or diabetic foot
New neurological deficit or asymmetric weakness requiring urgent neurological evaluation
Ulceration or infection over pressure points, especially with impaired perfusion or sensation
Rapidly evolving deformity with pain and swelling indicating inflammatory or neuropathic disease
reference.prognosis: When an underlying neuromuscular cause is stable, flexible claw toes respond well to tendon balancing and offloading, and fixed deformities improve with arthrodesis and metatarsophalangeal realignment. However, recurrence is more likely than with isolated hammer toe because the deforming intrinsic imbalance often persists, and outcomes depend heavily on recognising and managing the underlying disorder and protecting the insensate or ischaemic foot.
pitfalls: Treating clawing as an isolated toe problem and missing an underlying neuromuscular disorder or cavus foot
Failing to protect a neuropathic foot, allowing plantar callosities to progress to ulceration
Not assessing flexibility, leading to inappropriate soft-tissue surgery in a fixed deformity
Neglecting the plantarflexed metatarsal head and metatarsalgia when planning correction
Overlooking diabetes or vascular disease that compromises surgical healing
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Identification and management of the underlying neuromuscular cause such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or another peripheral neuropathy
Conservative measures including accommodative footwear with a wide, deep toe box, toe sleeves, orthoses and metatarsal pads or bars to offload the metatarsal heads, with regular callus care
Tendon-balancing surgery such as flexor-to-extensor transfer or tendon lengthening for flexible, passively correctable deformity
Bony correction with interphalangeal arthrodesis, metatarsophalangeal release and osteotomy for fixed deformity
Diabetic foot care and protective-sensation assessment to prevent ulceration over prominences
Neurology referral and nerve conduction studies where a neuromuscular cause is suspected
Podiatry and orthopaedic follow-up given the tendency to recurrence
